structured_output.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, then once introduced species and diadromous, euryhaline or marine-tolerant species are removed, essentially no native fresh-water fish species occur on two distant continents, while many species are shared between neighbouring river systems and countries within one continent.
structured_output.pass_criterion: Using FishBase native-status country checklists grouped into continents, take strictly fresh-water species (FishBase Fresh=1, excluding Brack and Saltwater tolerance flags and excluding anadromous or catadromous species). Count those with native status in two or more of the mutually distant continents South America, Africa, Asia, Australia and Europe. The claim passes if the count is 0, or if the shared fraction is below 0.5% of native fresh-water species and every shared case is shown to be a taxonomic or locality-record artefact. It must also hold that, within continents, at least 20% of species are native to more than one country (this checks the 'range widely' clause).
structured_output.fail_criterion: The claim fails if 5 or more strictly fresh-water, non-diadromous species are verified as native on two or more distant continents (excluding North America–Eurasia, which is treated as a sensitivity case only). It also fails if the shared fraction is 0.5% or more after manual checking of the flagged records, or if fewer than 20% of species are native to more than one country within a continent.
structured_output.interpretation: 'Fresh-water fish' means species that live in fresh water and do not use the sea for dispersal (strictly fresh-water, non-diadromous). 'Distant continents' means continents separated by ocean or by wide land and climate barriers: South America, Africa, Asia, Australia and Europe pairwise. North America and Eurasia are excluded from the main test because Holarctic species such as Esox lucius may span them, and they are analysed separately. 'Never' is read literally, with a tolerance only for data artefacts. Introduced populations are excluded because Darwin referred to natural distribution. Modern taxonomy may split species Darwin treated as one, which makes the test stricter than a nineteenth-century reading. 'Ranging widely and capriciously' is read as many species being native to several countries or basins within a continent, with partial overlap between basins.

dataset.name: FishBase
dataset.why_it_fits: FishBase records species-by-country checklists with a status field (native, introduced, endemic), plus salinity and habitat flags (freshwater, brackish, anadromous, catadromous). Country can be mapped to continent, which allows a direct count of native fresh-water species shared across continents. The same data show how many species are native to more than one country within a continent. The data are available through the Country and Species tables and the rfishbase R package.
